title: Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft: English Skeptical Masterwork
description: Reginald Scot published The Discoverie of Witchcraft in 1584, the most systematic English-language skeptical attack on witch prosecution. A Kentish gentleman with legal training, Scot argued from empirical observation, natural philosophy, and biblical interpretation that the phenomena attributed to witches had natural explanations, that confessions were produced by mental illness or deceit, and that the theological framework of diabolical witchcraft was a Catholic superstition incompatible with Protestant theology. Scot went further than Weyer, questioning the very reality of demonic interference in the physical world. When James VI became James I of England in 1603, he reportedly ordered all copies burned — though whether this order was carried out is disputed.
historiographical_note: Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons provides a revisionist reading of Scot, arguing against the standard interpretation of him as a proto-rationalist. Clark shows that Scot's skepticism operated within Protestant theological frameworks and that his dismissal of demonic intervention reflected a specific strain of Protestant natural philosophy rather than secular rationalism. The burning of Scot's books by James I demonstrates that the debate was theologically serious, not a contest between reason and superstition.
source_method: Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584); Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997); secondary scholarship
